paragraphs: Estimating body poses and tracking multiple people becomes difficult when movement blurs images or lighting is poor. The paper argues that existing RGB datasets mainly support more typical viewing conditions. This leaves a gap in the data available for developing systems that must recognize and follow people under these visual difficulties.

The authors introduce EHPT-XC, a dataset combining RGB images with event-camera data. Event cameras offer high dynamic range and microsecond temporal resolution, properties that make them promising for these conditions. The dataset includes motion blur from moving objects, low lighting, and situations where both problems occur together.

Including the two difficulties separately and jointly gives researchers several distinct settings for studying pose estimation and tracking. The contribution is a benchmark resource intended to support methods that use event information alongside conventional images. Its stated purpose is to encourage research on these extreme conditions; the abstract does not present a particular pose-estimation method as having solved them.
neurips-2024-a-benchmark-dataset-for-eve.tldr: EHPT-XC pairs RGB and event data to support human pose estimation and tracking under low light, motion blur, and their combination.

paragraphs: Causal fairness asks how sensitive attributes affect a model's decisions, rather than only comparing observed predictions across groups. Applying this idea becomes harder when the causal graph is only partially known. Several causal explanations may remain possible, so controlling unfairness requires accounting for that uncertainty while retaining useful predictions.

The paper proposes a min-max training framework for partially directed acyclic graphs. An efficient local procedure first estimates the possible effects of sensitive attributes on a prediction model using all possible adjustment sets. Training then alternates between updating the prediction model and the estimated causal effects, with a loss that controls the worst-case fairness violation.

This approach makes uncertainty about causal effects part of the training objective. The framework also extends to maximally oriented partially directed graphs when additional background knowledge is available. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support the authors' claims of improved performance, and the framework is presented as achieving interventional fairness with promising prediction accuracy.
neurips-2024-a-local-method-for-satisfyi.tldr: A local causal-effect estimation procedure supports min-max training that controls interventional unfairness when causal graphs are only partially known.

paragraphs: Differential privacy uses noise to limit information leakage from models trained on sensitive records. Choosing the noise scale affects both privacy and predictive usefulness. A common workflow selects a privacy budget, epsilon, calibrates noise to that budget, and then interprets epsilon through the risks posed by attacks on training records.

The authors show that this indirect calibration can give overly conservative assessments of attack risk. It can consequently introduce more noise than needed for the desired operational protection. Their alternative calibrates noise directly to a chosen attack-risk level, avoiding the intermediate step of selecting epsilon as the calibration target.

For a specified notion of attack risk, the proposed methods reduce noise while retaining the same risk level. Experiments using attack sensitivity and specificity as calibration targets report substantially better model accuracy. The result ties the utility improvement to the chosen definition of privacy risk: a tighter connection between noise and that risk allows more useful learning without weakening the specified protection.
neurips-2024-attack-aware-noise-calibrat.tldr: Calibrating privacy noise directly to a specified attack risk can improve model accuracy while preserving that risk level.

paragraphs: Structural inference tries to recover how parts of a dynamical system interact from observations of their behavior. Many methods address this problem within particular disciplines, making it difficult to compare their strengths objectively. This paper builds a shared benchmark to examine methods across different dynamics and interaction structures.

The study evaluates 13 methods using simulations spanning two kinds of dynamics and 11 interaction graph models. It also includes a biological experimental dataset to connect the comparison with a real application. Evaluation covers accuracy, scalability, robustness, and sensitivity to properties of the underlying graphs, rather than relying on a single measure of success.

The findings show that deep learning methods perform particularly well with multidimensional data, while approaches based on classical statistics and information theory are notably accurate and robust. Performance also correlates positively with average shortest path length in the interaction graph. These results provide evidence for choosing methods according to data and system characteristics, without establishing one approach as universally best.
neurips-2024-benchmarking-structural-inf.tldr: A benchmark of 13 structural inference methods reveals how their performance varies with data dimensionality and interaction-graph properties.

paragraphs: The Continuous Arcade Learning Environment, or CALE, extends the Arcade Learning Environment to support continuous actions. It retains Stella, the underlying Atari 2600 emulator. The central contribution is therefore a change in how agents can act within the environment suite, making it available for evaluating a broader range of reinforcement-learning approaches.

Continuous-action support allows continuous-control agents, including PPO and SAC, to be benchmarked alongside value-based agents such as DQN and Rainbow on the same suite. This shared setting creates an opportunity to study approaches that would otherwise be evaluated through different action interfaces. The environment itself becomes a common basis for those investigations.

The paper supplies initial results using Soft Actor-Critic and identifies research questions enabled by the extension. Those results establish a starting point for further evaluation rather than a general ranking of the listed algorithms. CALE is distributed as part of ALE, so the contribution combines an expanded experimental platform with initial evidence and directions for research.
neurips-2024-cale-continuous-arcade-lear.tldr: CALE adds continuous actions to Atari environments, enabling continuous-control and value-based agents to be evaluated on the same suite.

paragraphs: Understanding a procedure from video requires recognizing individual actions and how they fit into a larger sequence. Errors make this harder because a person may perform recognizable actions while deviating from the intended instructions. CaptainCook4D provides recordings designed to support research on that relationship between visible behavior, procedural structure, and mistakes.

The dataset contains 384 egocentric 4D recordings totaling 94.5 hours of people preparing recipes in real kitchens. It deliberately includes two kinds of activity: participants following the instructions and participants deviating from them to introduce errors. This provides examples of both intended execution and departures from the procedure.

The authors supply 5.3 thousand step annotations and 10 thousand fine-grained action annotations. They benchmark error recognition, multistep localization, and procedure learning, connecting the recordings to several aspects of procedural understanding. The contribution is a dataset and evaluation resource that treats mistakes as a central part of activity understanding, alongside the recognition of correctly performed actions and steps.
neurips-2024-captaincook4d-a-dataset-for.tldr: CaptainCook4D provides annotated cooking recordings with correct and deliberately erroneous execution for studying procedural understanding.

paragraphs: Distributionally robust optimization trains against uncertainty about the data distribution. This paper studies a penalized version with a closed, convex uncertainty set, a setting that includes f-DRO and spectral or L-risk minimization. The computational challenge is to coordinate model optimization with the opposing optimization over distributional uncertainty.

Drago is a stochastic primal-dual algorithm that combines cyclic and randomized components. Its distinctive feature is a carefully regularized update to the primal variables that helps reduce variance on the dual side. The design couples the two sides of the optimization problem, using the structure of one update to improve the behavior of the other.

For strongly convex-strongly concave DRO problems, the authors establish a state-of-the-art linear convergence rate. The bound tracks the primal and dual condition numbers separately, describing how each side's conditioning affects convergence. Numerical benchmarks on regression and classification support the theoretical analysis. The rate is specifically tied to the stated strong convexity and strong concavity conditions.
neurips-2024-drago-primal-dual-coupled-v.tldr: Drago couples primal and dual updates to achieve state-of-the-art linear convergence for strongly convex-strongly concave distributionally robust optimization.

paragraphs: Deep multi-view clustering combines different views of the same data to discover groups without supervision. Its success depends on how those views cooperate. The paper argues that existing approaches have not sufficiently examined each view's role in that cooperation, leaving room to improve how their information is fused.

The proposed SCE-MVC framework treats clustering as an unsupervised cooperative game, with each view acting as a participant. It uses Shapley values to assess the contributions of individual views. The utility used in this calculation comes from an optimal transport distance between the fused cluster distribution and a component associated with a single view.

The estimated contributions are then used to promote cooperation among views. This links the evaluation of a view's contribution to the way the framework encourages better fusion. Experiments applying the approach to existing deep multi-view clustering frameworks support its effectiveness. The findings suggest that explicitly evaluating cooperation can improve clustering, rather than treating the combination of views as sufficient on its own.
neurips-2024-evaluate-then-cooperate-sha.tldr: SCE-MVC uses Shapley values to evaluate individual views and strengthen their cooperation in deep multi-view clustering.

paragraphs: Visible-infrared person re-identification matches people across visible-light and infrared images. Attacks on these systems seek to disrupt the ranking of possible matches. The paper studies this security problem at the feature level, emphasizing that differences between imaging modalities create challenges beyond those found in single-modality person re-identification.

The method uses universal adversarial perturbations to represent disturbances shared across inputs. A Frequency-Spatial Attention Module combines frequency information with spatial focusing, emphasizing important regional features from the two domains within shared representations. This module is designed to keep the adversarial features consistent within the feature space while accounting for modality differences.

An auxiliary quadruple adversarial loss further amplifies differences between the modalities, causing incorrect output rankings. Experiments on SYSU-MM01 and RegDB, across different re-identification systems, support the attack's effectiveness. The contribution is evidence about vulnerabilities in cross-modality matching and a method for probing them, with the reported success grounded in the evaluated benchmarks and systems.
neurips-2024-feature-level-adversarial-a.tldr: Feature-level adversarial perturbations exploit visible-infrared differences to disrupt person re-identification rankings in benchmark experiments.

paragraphs: Unsupervised environment design trains a teacher to create environments that help a student agent learn. Existing approaches often use regret, the gap between optimal and actual performance, to select increasingly challenging experiences. The paper argues that this overlooks novelty: an environment can be challenging without expanding what the student has encountered.

CENIE measures novelty through the student's previous coverage of state-action space. This makes novelty depend on the curriculum experienced so far, rather than only on environment parameters, whose meaning can be underspecified. The authors implement the idea using Gaussian mixture models to represent coverage and assess how novel a candidate environment is.

The framework combines novelty and regret as complementary curriculum objectives. One encourages broader exploration, while the other supports increasing complexity. Adding CENIE to existing regret-based environment-design algorithms produces state-of-the-art performance across multiple evaluated benchmarks. These empirical results support the value of accounting for prior experience when creating curricula intended to improve generalization to unseen environments.
neurips-2024-improving-environment-novel.tldr: CENIE improves automated curricula by combining regret with novelty measured from the student's previous state-action coverage.

paragraphs: The prophet inequality studies when to accept a reward encountered in sequence. In the standard setting, a suitable threshold policy guarantees half the value available to an ideal prophet. This paper asks how much of that guarantee survives when each reward belongs to a player who selectively reveals information to improve their chance of selection.

The authors first characterize each player's optimal disclosure strategy. They define strategic robustness to require two guarantees: an approximation under strategic behavior and preservation of the usual one-half approximation when players are non-strategic. This definition evaluates protection against manipulation without giving up the standard guarantee in its absence.

For arbitrary reward distributions, they establish a tight robustness ratio of (1 − 1/e)/2. For independent, identically distributed rewards, a tight one-half robustness guarantee is achievable. One-half robustness is also achievable for non-identical log-concave distributions under certain regularity assumptions. Thus, the amount of protection available depends on distributional structure, with the final result explicitly conditional on those assumptions.
neurips-2024-intrinsic-robustness-of-pro.tldr: Threshold stopping policies retain provable approximation guarantees under strategic reward disclosure, with stronger guarantees for specified distribution classes.

paragraphs: LVX explains vision models using trees of linguistic attributes. The explanation method does not require model training. It connects language-generated concepts to the vision model's own representations, aiming to produce explanations that people can understand while remaining tied to how the particular model represents visual information.

An LLM proposes hierarchical visual attributes, and a text-to-image API supplies images aligned with those concepts. The collected text and images are mapped into the vision model's embedding space to form a visual embedding tree. Further LLM queries grow or prune that tree, adding useful attributes and removing unwanted concepts according to the model's representations.

For test samples, the resulting explanations take the form of attribute-rich trees. The authors also investigate a separate retraining application, calibrating a vision model on the generated hierarchy so it can incorporate the visual attribute knowledge. New benchmarks and evaluations support the explanations' plausibility, faithfulness, and stability. The training-free explanation process and the additional retraining application serve distinct purposes.
neurips-2024-language-model-as-visual-ex.tldr: LVX builds and adapts linguistic attribute trees to explain vision models without training the explanation model.

paragraphs: A generalized linear programming value function describes how an LP's optimal value changes as its objective and constraint bounds vary. Learning this function can support large-scale optimization, especially decomposition methods for two-stage mixed-integer linear programs. The paper develops a neural architecture from a structural characterization of the value function.

The learned model has three useful properties. It is a true under-approximation with respect to constraint bounds, is convex in those bounds, and can be trained without labels obtained by solving an LP for every example. Its structure also allows optimization over the trained model using linear programming, connecting approximation with subsequent decision-making.

Numerical results show good approximation even against supervised methods that require LP solutions for training data. The authors also develop a heuristic for large two-stage mixed-integer programs with continuous second-stage variables. Its compact reformulation is reported to solve faster than the full model's linear relaxation at large scales and orders of magnitude faster than the original model.
neurips-2024-learning-generalized-linear.tldr: A structurally constrained neural network learns LP value functions without solved-value labels and supports a fast heuristic for large two-stage optimization problems.

paragraphs: Membership inference asks whether a particular record was used to train a model. The paper identifies two weaknesses in existing attacks on language models: reference-based calibration depends on suitably matched reference data, and probability-based membership signals depend heavily on overfitting. Regularization and generalization can weaken that signal and contribute to false positives.

SPV-MIA addresses both issues. Its self-prompt procedure queries the target language model to collect data for fine-tuning a reference model, helping align the reference data distribution through public API access. It also introduces probabilistic variation as a membership signal grounded in memorization rather than relying on high sampling probability alone.

The authors provide theoretical grounding that reconnects this signal with the neighbour attack. Evaluations across three datasets and four language models report an increase in attack AUC from 0.7 to 0.9. This is evidence of stronger membership discrimination in those experiments, highlighting how reference-data construction and the choice of signal affect estimates of privacy exposure.
neurips-2024-membership-inference-attack.tldr: SPV-MIA combines self-prompted reference data with a memorization-based signal, raising membership-inference AUC from 0.7 to 0.9 in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Flow-matching generative models rely on paths that connect source and target distributions. Straight paths are natural under Euclidean geometry, but they can pass outside the data manifold. For trajectory inference, that can produce interpolations that fail to reflect the dynamics responsible for the observed starting and ending distributions.

Metric Flow Matching changes the geometry used to construct these paths. It learns approximate geodesics by minimizing kinetic energy under a Riemannian metric induced by the data. The resulting simulation-free framework trains the generative model to match vector fields on the data manifold, which the authors associate with lower uncertainty and more meaningful interpolations.

The paper provides general, task-independent metrics and evaluates the framework on LiDAR navigation, unpaired image translation, and cellular dynamics. It reports improvements over Euclidean baselines and state-of-the-art results for single-cell trajectory prediction. These findings support the usefulness of data-informed path geometry, particularly when the intermediate trajectory is an important part of the task.
neurips-2024-metric-flow-matching-for-sm.tldr: Metric Flow Matching learns paths under data-induced geometry to produce more meaningful interpolations and improve trajectory-related tasks.

paragraphs: Routing with uncertain travel times requires deciding what kind of bad outcome to guard against. This paper uses min-max regret: it seeks a route whose largest shortfall relative to the best route for the realized scenario is as small as possible. The formulation extends both traveling salesman and vehicle routing problems.

A general budget uncertainty set describes the uncertain travel times and allows control over solution conservatism. It includes interval uncertainty as a special case. The proposed neural method uses dual multi-head cross attention to extract features from these uncertainty sets, making the uncertainty representation part of the model's input.

To handle the maximization embedded in the regret objective, the method invokes a pretrained model to derive a regret value and uses it as a training reward. Experiments on robust traveling salesman and vehicle routing instances support its effectiveness across different sizes. The authors report shorter solution times than alternative heuristics, providing empirical evidence for neural approaches to this robust routing formulation.
neurips-2024-neural-combinatorial-optimi.tldr: A neural routing method represents travel-time uncertainty explicitly and uses regret-based training to efficiently solve robust routing instances.

paragraphs: Best-arm identification seeks the best option while controlling the probability of a wrong answer. In the batched version, the learner also wants to change its sampling policy infrequently. The paper studies how to minimize both the total number of samples and the number of batches while achieving success probability at least 1 − delta.

Tri-BBAI achieves optimal asymptotic sample complexity as delta approaches zero and uses three batches in expectation. Building on it, Opt-BBAI achieves near-optimal sample and batch complexity when the inverse error tolerance is finite. As delta approaches zero, Opt-BBAI retains the same sample and batch complexity as Tri-BBAI.

A further distinction concerns unsuccessful runs. Earlier non-asymptotic batch bounds often condition on returning the best arm, leaving complexity potentially unbounded when an inferior arm is returned. Opt-BBAI's bounds do not depend on that success event. A procedure for checking whether the best arm has been eliminated enables this stronger accounting of resource use.
neurips-2024-optimal-batched-best-arm-id.tldr: Tri-BBAI and Opt-BBAI identify the best arm with optimal or near-optimal sampling and batching guarantees under their respective regimes.

paragraphs: Bayesian algorithm execution tries to infer the output of an algorithm when evaluating its underlying function is expensive. Running that algorithm directly may require too many evaluations. Instead, the framework chooses evaluation points sequentially using probabilistic information about the function, concentrating resources on learning the property of interest.

Existing approaches guide this choice through expected information gain, which can itself be computationally demanding. PS-BAX uses posterior sampling as a simpler alternative. It draws on the observation that many desired properties correspond to a target set of points defined by the function, covering tasks such as optimization variants and level-set estimation.

Across diverse experiments, PS-BAX is competitive with existing baselines while being substantially faster, easier to implement, and readily parallelizable. The authors also establish conditions under which it converges asymptotically. Together, the empirical results and conditional theory support posterior sampling as a practical way to allocate expensive evaluations toward a specific algorithmic output.
neurips-2024-practical-bayesian-algorith.tldr: PS-BAX uses posterior sampling to select expensive function evaluations, matching baseline performance with lower computational overhead in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Training-data poisoning introduces adversarial examples that can make a learned model misclassify inputs. Existing defenses can reduce generalization, depend on the particular attack, or add substantial training overhead. PureGen addresses this problem by purifying training data through generative-model dynamics, aiming to remove harmful alterations while retaining useful information for classification.

The authors propose stochastic transformations implemented with iterative Langevin dynamics of energy-based models, denoising diffusion probabilistic models, or combinations of the two. These specially trained generative models process poisoned data without requiring attack-specific or classifier-specific information. The approach therefore seeks a shared purification mechanism across different poisoning settings.

Experiments report state-of-the-art defenses against attacks including Narcissus, Bullseye Polytope, and Gradient Matching on CIFAR-10, Tiny-ImageNet, and CINIC-10, with minimal impact on classifier generalization. The paper also examines performance trade-offs and finds the methods remain highly effective when the generative models' own training data are poisoned or distributionally shifted. These claims describe the evaluated settings rather than a guarantee against every attack.
neurips-2024-puregen-universal-data-puri.tldr: PureGen uses generative-model dynamics to purify poisoned training data without attack- or classifier-specific information.

paragraphs: Diffusion-based video super-resolution can produce realistic-looking frames, but random fluctuations can make details inconsistent over time. The paper argues that conventional pixel alignment is ineffective when iterative diffusion repeatedly disrupts those pixels. SeeClear addresses this issue through semantic controls that guide conditional video generation across frames.

Its Semantic Distiller and Pixel Condenser work together to extract and upscale semantic details from low-resolution video. The Instance-Centric Alignment Module uses tokens shared across a video clip to relate pixels within and between frames. A Channel-wise Texture Aggregation Memory adds external knowledge through persistent semantic textures, giving the framework another source of guidance.

SeeClear also incorporates the ResShift mechanism into its blurring diffusion process to balance sharpness and diffusion effects. Experiments report an advantage over state-of-the-art diffusion-based video super-resolution methods. The contribution combines several forms of semantic guidance with a modified diffusion process, supporting the authors' approach to improving detail coherence alongside perceptual quality in the evaluated videos.
neurips-2024-seeclear-semantic-distillat.tldr: SeeClear combines semantic alignment, texture memory, and a modified diffusion process to improve video super-resolution consistency.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can perform well on image and language tasks while still struggling with spatial arrangements. SpatialRGPT targets the ability to reason about regions' relative directions and distances. It connects regional visual representations with three-dimensional scene information so that spatial relationships become an explicit focus of learning.

The method has two main components: a data-curation pipeline based on 3D scene graphs and a flexible module that adds depth information to an existing model's visual encoder. At inference time, users can specify regions for spatial comparison. The paper also introduces SpatialRGBT-Bench, with ground-truth 3D annotations from indoor, outdoor, and simulated environments.

Results show substantial improvements in spatial reasoning both with and without local region prompts. The authors also report strong generalization to complex spatial relations and demonstrate use as a region-aware dense reward annotator for robotic tasks. These findings connect improved spatial representations to both answering relationship questions and providing spatially grounded feedback for robotics.
neurips-2024-spatialrgpt-grounded-spatia.tldr: SpatialRGPT combines 3D scene-graph training data and depth integration to improve vision-language models' spatial reasoning.

paragraphs: Sampling-based accounts of perception propose that stochastic cortical activity represents uncertainty by sampling possible explanations of a stimulus. Many circuit models leave out the diversity of inhibitory neurons. This paper studies how two inhibitory cell types could contribute differently to Bayesian sampling within a nonlinear recurrent circuit.

The model contains excitatory neurons arranged as a ring attractor, PV neurons supplying global inhibition, and SOM neurons supplying local inhibition that depends on tuning. By analyzing the circuit dynamics, the authors identify the sampling algorithms those dynamics implement. The reduced circuit containing only excitatory and PV neurons performs Langevin sampling.

Adding tuning-dependent SOM inhibition changes the dynamics to Hamiltonian sampling and speeds sampling in the model. The Hamiltonian interpretation also requires SOM neurons to lack direct feedforward connections, a condition the authors describe as consistent with neuroanatomy. The result is a theoretical connection between inhibitory circuit organization and computational sampling, offering an account of how interneuron diversity may support Bayesian inference.
neurips-2024-the-bayesian-sampling-in-a-.tldr: A recurrent circuit model links PV inhibition to Langevin sampling and the addition of SOM inhibition to faster Hamiltonian sampling.

paragraphs: Bayesian estimators can have strong guarantees when the data prior is known, but that prior is often unavailable. Algorithm unrolling addresses this by making neural-network layers resemble iterations of an inference algorithm and training them on examples. The paper asks whether this process can provably recover the behavior of an optimal, prior-aware method.

The authors establish learning guarantees for networks built by unrolling approximate message passing. For compressed sensing with training data drawn from a product prior, they prove that the network layers approximately converge to the denoisers used by Bayes AMP. This connects learning from examples with the denoising operations that explicit prior knowledge would prescribe.

Numerical experiments cover compressed sensing and rank-one matrix estimation. They demonstrate adaptation to general priors and improvements over Bayes AMP in settings involving low dimensions, non-Gaussian designs, and non-product priors. Those broader observations are empirical; the stated compressed-sensing learning guarantee specifically assumes a product prior. The work therefore combines a conditional theoretical result with evidence across more general settings.
neurips-2024-unrolled-denoising-networks.tldr: Under a product-prior assumption, unrolled AMP networks provably learn denoisers approximating those of Bayes AMP, with broader benefits demonstrated experimentally.

paragraphs: Benign overfitting describes a situation in which a model overfits its training data yet still performs well on unseen examples. This paper investigates that phenomenon for a vision-oriented Transformer. Its aim is to explain theoretically when fitting the training set is compatible with good generalization in the model under study.

The analysis considers a Transformer with one softmax self-attention layer followed by a fully connected layer, trained by gradient descent under a particular data-distribution model. The authors develop techniques for handling softmax and the dependence between multiple trainable weights. These allow them to characterize training dynamics and analyze generalization after training.

The central result is a sharp condition based on the data model's signal-to-noise ratio that separates small-test-error and large-test-error regimes. Experimental simulations support the theoretical findings. This provides a specific account of when benign overfitting occurs for the analyzed architecture and distribution, with the scope of the conclusion tied to that mathematical setting.
neurips-2024-unveil-benign-overfitting-f.tldr: A theoretical analysis identifies a signal-to-noise condition separating good and poor generalization for an overfitted Transformer under a specified data model.

paragraphs: Conditional average treatment effects describe how an intervention's average effect varies with observed characteristics. Choosing an estimator is difficult because observational data do not reveal the counterfactual outcome needed for ordinary validation. Existing selection metrics can also require auxiliary models and may not specifically favor estimators that remain useful under distribution shifts.

The paper introduces a Distributionally Robust Metric for selecting CATE estimators. DRM avoids fitting nuisance models, such as outcome or propensity models, as part of its selection procedure. It is designed to prioritize distributional robustness, making resilience to changes in the data distribution an explicit criterion for comparing candidate estimators.

Experiments support DRM's effectiveness in selecting estimators robust to shifts associated with changing covariates and hidden confounders. The contribution concerns model selection: it provides a way to prefer robust treatment-effect estimators without the additional nuisance-model fitting required by the discussed alternatives. The empirical findings support that selection capability in the evaluated shift settings.
neurips-2024-unveiling-the-potential-of-.tldr: DRM selects treatment-effect estimators without nuisance-model fitting and empirically favors robustness to covariate shifts and hidden confounders.
